title: Phrasal Verbs with In and Out
summary: Use in and out to describe entering and leaving places, distinguish these particles from into and out of before a destination, and apply everyday combinations for visits, participation, power, forms, restaurants, dropping out and omitting information.
learningObjectives: Choose in or out for movement into or away from an understood place, and use into or out of before a named place.
Use check in, check out, move in, move out and let somebody in or out in realistic situations.
Use drop in, join in, plug in, fill in or out and take somebody in with their appropriate meanings and objects.
Use eat out, drop out of, get out of, leave out and cross out without confusing omission, withdrawal and avoidance.

explanation.heading: In and out for entering and leaving
explanation.body: In can indicate movement into an understood place, and out can indicate movement away from it: come in, step out, move in, get out. When the place is stated, it is common to use into or out of: step into the room, get out of the car. These patterns convey a difference between an unstated destination and a named one.
explanation.example: The guard opened the side door and invited the visitors in.

explanation.heading: Moving and checking in or out
explanation.body: Move in means begin living in a home; move out means leave a home permanently or for a new place. Move into a flat and move out of a house explicitly name the places involved. At a hotel, check in means register on arrival, while check out means complete departure arrangements. Avoid mixing the hotel sense with checkout in a shop.
explanation.example: We checked out early and moved into the rented cottage that afternoon.

explanation.heading: Visiting, participating and connecting devices
explanation.body: Drop in is an informal, usually unplanned short visit, often followed by on someone or to see someone. Join in means take part in an activity already happening. Plug in a device, or plug it in, means connect it to power. These expressions do different jobs despite sharing the particle in.
explanation.example: When the workshop began, two neighbours dropped in and joined in the discussion.

explanation.heading: Completing information and recognising deception
explanation.body: Fill in and fill out can both mean complete a form by entering the required details. With a pronoun, say fill it in or fill it out. Take somebody in can mean deceive somebody into believing a false claim: the person is taken in by the story. This meaning is separate from allowing someone to enter a place.
explanation.example: The online message looked convincing, but it did not take the cautious buyer in.

explanation.heading: Out for eating elsewhere, leaving or removing
explanation.body: Eat out means have a meal away from home, normally in a restaurant. Drop out of a course or competition means stop participating before completing it; get out of an agreed duty means avoid doing it. Leave something out means omit a detail, while cross something out means draw a line through words to delete them. In these separable combinations, say leave it out and cross it out.
explanation.example: The editor crossed out the incorrect date but left the rest of the paragraph unchanged.

left.label: In or out alone
left.note: The place being left is understood from context.

right.label: Out of + named place
right.example: The swimmer climbed out of the pool.
right.note: Out of introduces the place from which the swimmer emerged.

comparisons.title: Leaving a course versus leaving a detail

left.label: Drop out of + activity
left.example: Jules dropped out of the evening class.
left.note: The person stopped participating before the course ended.

right.label: Leave out + information
right.example: Jules left out the final paragraph.
right.note: Information was omitted from a text; it was not a withdrawal from a course.

examples.sentence: The residents moved into their new apartment at the start of September.
examples.note: Into directly introduces the named new home.

examples.sentence: Visitors must check in at reception before entering the exhibition hall.
examples.note: Check in names arrival and registration.

examples.sentence: Everyone was already singing when I joined in.
examples.note: Join in means start participating in something under way.

examples.sentence: Please plug the projector in before the audience arrives.
examples.note: Plug in is separable with a noun object.

examples.sentence: The applicant left her middle name out of the online form by mistake.
examples.note: Leave out means omit information, whether deliberately or accidentally.

commonMistakes.incorrect: We are moving in our new house on Saturday.
commonMistakes.correct: We are moving into our new house on Saturday.
commonMistakes.why: Move into a named property uses into; move in alone can leave the destination unstated.

commonMistakes.incorrect: He dropped out from the language course in March.
commonMistakes.correct: He dropped out of the language course in March.
commonMistakes.why: Drop out of is the standard fixed pattern for withdrawing from a course.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Please plug in it before you start the demonstration.
commonMistakes.correct: Please plug it in before you start the demonstration.
commonMistakes.why: The pronoun it belongs between plug and in in this separable phrasal verb.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I accidentally crossed out it on the form.
commonMistakes.correct: I accidentally crossed it out on the form.
commonMistakes.why: Cross out is separable; put the object pronoun before out.

studyTips: Practise four directions with a room: go in, go into the room, go out, go out of the room.
Organise in/out verbs by context: hotel (check in/out), devices (plug in), visits (drop in) and forms (fill in/out).
Contrast similar-looking meanings aloud: drop out of a class, get out of a duty, leave out a name, and cross out an incorrect word.

exercises.prompt: The guests have arrived at their hotel and want their room keys. They need to ___.
exercises.feedback: Hotel guests check in when registering on arrival; check out is done on departure.

exercises.prompt: The new tenant signed the agreement and is moving ___ the apartment on Monday.
exercises.feedback: Move into + a named home expresses entering it to live there; move in can stand alone.

exercises.prompt: The team had already started the game, but Priya wanted to ___ and play too.
exercises.feedback: Join in means start participating in an activity that has already begun.

exercises.prompt: This date is incorrect. Use a pen to ___ and write the correct one next to it.
exercises.feedback: Cross it out means draw a line through it, and the pronoun must appear before out.

exercises.prompt: The dining room was closed, so we decided to ___ at a nearby restaurant. (Use the two-word verb for having a restaurant meal.)
acceptedAnswers: eat out
exercises.feedback: Eat out means have a meal away from home, usually at a restaurant.

exercises.prompt: Nora started the course but ___ after the first month. (Write the past-simple form of drop out; two words.)
acceptedAnswers: dropped out
exercises.feedback: Dropped out means Nora left the course without completing it.

exercises.prompt: We had not arranged a visit, but we ___ to see our neighbours on the way home. (Use the past simple of drop in; two words.)
acceptedAnswers: dropped in
exercises.feedback: Dropped in means paid an informal visit without arranging it in advance.

exercises.prompt: The tablet needs power. Please plug ___ before the lesson. (Use the pronoun it and particle in.)
acceptedAnswers: it in
exercises.feedback: Plug it in places the pronoun between the verb and particle.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: They are moving in their new flat this weekend.
acceptedAnswers: They are moving into their new flat this weekend.
exercises.feedback: When naming the home after move, use into: move into the flat.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: She filled on the application form before lunch.
acceptedAnswers: She filled in the application form before lunch.
She filled out the application form before lunch.
exercises.feedback: Both fill in and fill out are standard for completing a form; fill on is not.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: Please leave out it when you prepare the short summary.
acceptedAnswers: Please leave it out when you prepare the short summary.
exercises.feedback: The object pronoun it comes between leave and out.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The dog ran out the kitchen when the door opened.
acceptedAnswers: The dog ran out of the kitchen when the door opened.
exercises.feedback: Use out of before the named room: ran out of the kitchen. Out alone works when the place is left unstated.

speakingExercises.prompt: You have arrived at your hotel and need to register. Say one sentence starting “I need to” and ending “now”, using check in.
acceptedAnswers: I need to check in now.
speakingExercises.feedback: Check in names the action guests take when they arrive at a hotel.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say one past-simple sentence with these facts: Ella / move into / her new flat / last Friday. Begin with “Ella”.
acceptedAnswers: Ella moved into her new flat last Friday.
speakingExercises.feedback: Moved into identifies the named new home.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct only the object position in this sentence and say it aloud: “Please plug in it before the meeting.”
acceptedAnswers: Please plug it in before the meeting.
speakingExercises.feedback: Plug it in places the pronoun between verb and particle.

speakingExercises.prompt: Rephrase “We had dinner at a restaurant rather than at home” using eat out. Begin with “We” and use the past simple. Do not mention the restaurant.
acceptedAnswers: We ate out.
speakingExercises.feedback: Ate out expresses eating a meal away from home.

speakingExercises.prompt: Tell a friend to participate in an activity already happening. Use the complete instruction “Please join in the discussion.”
acceptedAnswers: Please join in the discussion.
speakingExercises.feedback: Join in the discussion means start taking part in it.

speakingExercises.prompt: Describe this withdrawal in one sentence: Ravi / drop out of / the training course / in June. Use the past simple and begin with “Ravi”.
acceptedAnswers: Ravi dropped out of the training course in June.
speakingExercises.feedback: Drop out of expresses leaving a course before completion.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two sentences in this order using the facts given. First: “the team / check in / at noon” (past simple). Second: “they / check out / the next morning” (past simple). Use full forms.
acceptedAnswers: The team checked in at noon. They checked out the next morning.
speakingExercises.feedback: Checked in is hotel arrival registration; checked out is departure.

speakingExercises.prompt: An editor asks what you did to an inaccurate sentence. Reply in one past-simple sentence beginning “I” and ending “of the report”. Use leave out, replacing the sentence with the object pronoun it.
acceptedAnswers: I left it out of the report.
speakingExercises.feedback: Left it out of the report is the natural expression for omitting a sentence; it goes before out.

listeningExercises.audioText: I have just arrived at the hostel. I will check in now and collect my key from reception.
listeningExercises.prompt: What is the speaker about to do?
listeningExercises.feedback: Check in at a hostel involves arrival and registration.

listeningExercises.audioText: Mara moved out of her old apartment on Thursday and moved into a smaller one on Saturday.
listeningExercises.prompt: Where did Mara move on Saturday?
listeningExercises.feedback: Moved into identifies the new place she began living in on Saturday.

listeningExercises.audioText: When the music started, our neighbours joined in and danced with everyone else.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word past-simple phrasal verb immediately after “neighbours”.
acceptedAnswers: joined in
listeningExercises.feedback: Joined in means they became participants in the activity.

listeningExercises.audioText: The form was almost complete, but Theo left out the phone number by mistake.
listeningExercises.prompt: What was missing from the form?
listeningExercises.feedback: Left out means omitted; the missing information was the phone number.

listeningExercises.audioText: The online advert looked official, but the company had invented the story. Several people were taken in.
listeningExercises.feedback: Taken in here means misled into believing a false story.

listeningExercises.audioText: I was meant to give the welcome speech, but a colleague offered to do it, so I got out of giving it.
listeningExercises.prompt: What did the speaker avoid doing?
listeningExercises.feedback: Got out of giving it means the speaker no longer had to deliver the speech.

listeningExercises.audioText: At reception, we checked out before breakfast because our train left early.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word past-simple phrasal verb immediately after “we”.
acceptedAnswers: checked out
listeningExercises.feedback: Checked out describes the formal end of a hotel stay.

listeningExercises.audioText: The teacher asked me to cross it out because the date was wrong.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word phrasal-verb phrase immediately after “to”.
acceptedAnswers: cross it out
listeningExercises.feedback: Cross it out puts the object pronoun in the middle and means mark it for deletion.
